# Start with five units to deliver

Imagine that vertex `1` has material to send to vertex `4`. An arrow's
capacity is the most material it can carry. Vertices `2` and `3` may forward
material, but cannot create or keep it. How much can reach `4` altogether?

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=9mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick},lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt}]
\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (3,1.3) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (3,-1.3) {3};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (6,0) {4};
\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab]{3}(a);
\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab]{2}(b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab]{1}(b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab]{2}(t);
\draw[ar] (b)--node[lab]{4}(t);
\node[below=5mm] at (s.south) {source};
\node[below=5mm] at (t.south) {sink};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Start with nothing on any arrow. We will build a delivery by choosing one
complete route at a time. For now, follow the amounts in the drawings; we
will study how an algorithm finds its routes later.

In the next three drawings, each label is **amount already sent / capacity**,
after the step. For example, `2/3` means that the arrow carries `2` units and
can still carry `1` more. Blue arrows show the route used in that step; the
other arrows keep their previous amounts.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{8cm}
```

## First route: send two units through vertex 2

Choose `1 -> 2 -> 4`. The first arrow can carry `3` units, but the second
can carry only `2`. Send **2 units along both arrows**: vertex 2 receives
2 and immediately forwards 2 to vertex 4. Sending 3 would overload `2 -> 4`.

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=9mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 chosen/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt}]
\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (2.6,1.1) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (2.6,-1.1) {3};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (5.2,0) {4};
\draw[chosen] (s)--node[lab] {$\mathbf{2}/3$} (a);
\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab] {$0/2$} (b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab] {$0/1$} (b);
\draw[chosen] (a)--node[lab] {$\mathbf{2}/2$} (t);
\draw[ar] (b)--node[lab] {$0/4$} (t);
\node[anchor=west,align=left,text width=5.1cm,
        font=\small] at (6.2,0) {\textbf{Added on this route: 2}\\[4pt]\textbf{Total delivered: 2}\\[8pt]Vertex 2: $2$ arrives, $2$ leaves.\\[4pt]Edge $2\to4$ is now full.\\Edge $1\to2$ still has room for $1$.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

```{=latex}
\Needspace{8cm}
```

## Second route: send two more units through vertex 3

Keep the first delivery in place. On `1 -> 3 -> 4`, neither arrow has been
used yet: they have room for `2` and `4` units respectively. Send **2 more
units along both arrows**. The receiver now gets 2 through vertex 2 and
2 through vertex 3, for a total of 4.

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=9mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 chosen/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt}]
\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (2.6,1.1) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (2.6,-1.1) {3};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (5.2,0) {4};
\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab] {$2/3$} (a);
\draw[chosen] (s)--node[lab] {$\mathbf{2}/2$} (b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab] {$0/1$} (b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab] {$2/2$} (t);
\draw[chosen] (b)--node[lab] {$\mathbf{2}/4$} (t);
\node[anchor=west,align=left,text width=5.1cm,
        font=\small] at (6.2,0) {\textbf{Added on this route: 2}\\[4pt]\textbf{Total delivered: 4}\\[8pt]Vertex 3: $2$ arrives, $2$ leaves.\\[4pt]Edge $1\to3$ is now full.\\Edge $3\to4$ still has room for $2$.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10cm}
```

## Third route: use the remaining room between the branches

Four is not the limit. Although `2 -> 4` is full, we can still go from
vertex 2 through vertex 3 to reach vertex 4. Look at the previous drawing:

- `1 -> 2` carries 2 of its capacity 3: room for **1** more.
- `2 -> 3` carries 0 of its capacity 1: room for **1** more.
- `3 -> 4` carries 2 of its capacity 4: room for **2** more.

So route `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4` can carry **1 additional unit**. Add it on each
of these three arrows, leaving every other amount unchanged:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=9mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 chosen/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt}]
\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (2.6,1.1) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (2.6,-1.1) {3};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (5.2,0) {4};
\draw[chosen] (s)--node[lab] {$\mathbf{3}/3$} (a);
\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab] {$2/2$} (b);
\draw[chosen] (a)--node[lab] {$\mathbf{1}/1$} (b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab] {$2/2$} (t);
\draw[chosen] (b)--node[lab] {$\mathbf{3}/4$} (t);
\node[anchor=west,align=left,text width=5.1cm,
        font=\small] at (6.2,0) {\textbf{Added on this route: 1}\\[4pt]\textbf{Total delivered: 5}\\[8pt]Vertex 2: $3$ arrives, $2+1$ leaves.\\[4pt]Vertex 3: $2+1$ arrives, $3$ leaves.\\[4pt]Both junctions still balance.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

The amount an entire route can add is limited by its smallest remaining
room. This amount is called its **bottleneck**: here it was 2, then 2, then 1.
Notice that the final labels show the accumulated amounts, not just the last
unit added: `1 -> 2` now carries 3, and `3 -> 4` now carries 3.

## Why five is the maximum

The receiver gets `2 + 3 = 5`. No larger delivery is possible because the
only arrows leaving vertex 1 have capacities `3` and `2`, and both are full.
Even though `3 -> 4` still has room for one more unit, no additional unit can
leave the source to reach it.

We have both a feasible routing of 5 units and an upper bound of 5. This is
the basic proof pattern we will reuse for maximum flow.

## Vocabulary for the example

A **flow network** is a directed graph, a nonnegative capacity for each input
edge, and distinct vertices `s` (source) and `t` (sink). Each input edge has
its own flow, even when several arrows have the same endpoints.

A feasible flow satisfies two rules:

```text
0 <= flow[edge] <= capacity[edge]
for each vertex except s and t: total incoming flow = total outgoing flow
```

The **flow value** measures how much the source supplies to the sink. In our
final drawing, it is **5**: `3 + 2` leaves vertex 1, and `2 + 3` reaches
vertex 4. Do not add the amounts on every edge of the graph: that would count
the same unit again each time it passes through another edge.

**A return to the source must be subtracted.** Some networks have actual input edges
returning to the source. In the drawing below, the source sends 7 units to
`u`, but `u` sends 2 back and forwards only 5 to the sink. The value is
therefore **7 - 2 = 5**, not 7. Labels here are the amounts carried; capacities
are omitted. Both opposite arrows are real input edges.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{5cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=9mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick},lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt}]
\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {$s$};
\node[nd] (u) at (4,0) {$u$};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (8,0) {$t$};
\draw[ar] (s) to[bend left=25] node[lab,above] {$7$} (u);
\draw[ar] (u) to[bend left=25] node[lab,below] {$2$} (s);
\draw[ar] (u)--node[lab,above] {$5$}(t);
\node[below=11mm,align=center,font=\small] at (s.south)
 {supplies $7-2=5$};
\node[below=11mm,align=center,font=\small] at (u.south)
 {receives $7$, forwards $2+5$};
\node[below=11mm,align=center,font=\small] at (t.south)
 {receives $5$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

This gives the general definition:

```text
flow value = total leaving s - total returning to s
           = total entering t - total leaving t
```

The two calculations agree because every intermediate vertex forwards exactly
what it receives: it creates nothing and keeps nothing. The amount supplied
by the source must therefore equal the amount absorbed by the sink. If no
input edge enters `s` or leaves `t`, as in our opening network, the subtracted
amounts are simply zero.

**The optimization goal.** We want the largest flow value among all
assignments satisfying the capacity and conservation rules. We can start with
zero on every edge: no capacity is exceeded, and each junction receives and
forwards zero. We will then improve this assignment while keeping both rules
true.

A maximum flow need not fill every edge. In the opening example, `3 -> 4`
carries only 3 of its capacity 4, yet the value 5 is maximum because no more
can leave the source. The algorithm maintains the edge amounts; an exercise
asking only for the maximum value needs just the number `5` as output.

# Reversible choices let us repair a routing

In the opening example, we never changed an amount already assigned to an
edge. We now examine a strategy that repeatedly chooses a route with room
left and sends flow along it. An early route can be perfectly feasible yet
need revising later. Consider this network, where every capacity is `1`.

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick},sel/.style={->,very thick,blue!65!black},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small}]
\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (2.5,1.3) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (2.5,-1.3) {3};
\node[nd] (c) at (5,1.3) {4};
\node[nd] (d) at (5,-1.3) {5};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (7.5,0) {6};
\draw[sel] (s)--node[lab]{1/1}(a);
\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab]{0/1}(b);
\draw[sel] (a)--node[lab]{1/1}(c);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab,pos=.65]{0/1}(d);
\draw[ar] (b)--node[lab,pos=.65]{0/1}(c);
\draw[sel] (c)--node[lab]{1/1}(t);
\draw[ar] (d)--node[lab]{0/1}(t);
\node[align=center] at (3.75,-2.3)
 {After choosing route $1\to2\to4\to6$.\\Labels are flow/capacity.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

The route `1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 6` carries one unit and respects every rule.
But keeping it unchanged blocks further delivery: the remaining branch
`1 -> 3 -> 4` cannot reach the sink because `4 -> 6` is full, and `1 -> 2`
is also full. A search restricted to unused forward capacity stops at value 1.

## A different first choice would succeed

We could instead have chosen `1 -> 2 -> 5 -> 6` first, then
`1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 6`. These two routes fit together and deliver 2 units:

```{=latex}
\Needspace{5cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 first/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 second/.style={->,very thick,draw=green!40!black},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small}]
\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (2.5,1.3) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (2.5,-1.3) {3};
\node[nd] (c) at (5,1.3) {4};
\node[nd] (d) at (5,-1.3) {5};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (7.5,0) {6};
\draw[first] (s)--node[lab]{1/1}(a);
\draw[second] (s)--node[lab]{1/1}(b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab]{0/1}(c);
\draw[first] (a)--node[lab,pos=.65]{1/1}(d);
\draw[second] (b)--node[lab,pos=.65]{1/1}(c);
\draw[second] (c)--node[lab]{1/1}(t);
\draw[first] (d)--node[lab]{1/1}(t);
\node[align=center,font=\small] at (3.75,-2.3)
 {Blue: $1\to2\to5\to6$. Green: $1\to3\to4\to6$.\\
  Total delivered: 2. Labels are flow/capacity.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

So cancellation is not required in every execution. On this graph, a good
first choice avoids it. The issue is how to choose a first route before we
know the final arrangement. All three initial routes have three edges and a
bottleneck of 1; choosing a shortest route or a route with the largest
bottleneck does not distinguish the unfortunate choice from the other two.

## Let an early choice remain provisional

We want a method that can take a feasible route without first proving that
it belongs to some optimal final routing. To achieve that, earlier amounts
must remain adjustable. Otherwise, after the first drawing, the method would
incorrectly conclude that no improvement is possible.

We could abandon earlier routes and try alternatives. The residual graph
provides a systematic way to express just the adjustments needed. In this
example, keep the unit on `1 -> 2` and `4 -> 6`, cancel its use of `2 -> 4`,
and add flow on the other branch edges. That produces exactly the two-unit
routing in the second drawing. The next subsection explains how one search
can describe all those changes together.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12cm}
```

## Residual capacity means permission to change flow

For an input edge `u -> v` with capacity `c` and current flow `f`, maintain
**two residual edges**:

The forward residual arrow `u -> v` has capacity `c - f`: room to add more
flow. The backward residual arrow `v -> u` has capacity `f`: room to cancel
flow already assigned to this input edge.

For capacity `7` and current flow `5`, these permissions are `2` and `5`.
The two rows below show what changes when we use the backward permission to
cancel `3` units:


```{=latex}
% Residual permissions before and after cancellation
\Needspace{8cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!40,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[note,anchor=west] at (-.4,2.1) {Input edge: flow/capacity};
\node[note,anchor=west] at (5.1,2.1) {Residual pair: permitted changes};
\node[nd] (a) at (0,1) {$u$};
\node[nd] (b) at (2.4,1) {$v$};
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab,above] {$5/7$}(b);
\draw[ar] (3.1,1)--(4.1,1);
\node[nd] (c) at (5.2,1) {$u$};
\node[nd] (d) at (8.6,1) {$v$};
\draw[blue] (c) to[bend left=26] node[lab,above] {add up to 2} (d);
\draw[undo] (d) to[bend left=26] node[lab,below] {cancel up to 5} (c);
\node[note,anchor=west] at (-.4,-.5)
 {Cancel 3 units of the input edge's flow. Its capacity remains 7.};
\node[nd] (e) at (0,-2) {$u$};
\node[nd] (f) at (2.4,-2) {$v$};
\draw[ar] (e)--node[lab,above] {$2/7$}(f);
\draw[ar] (3.1,-2)--(4.1,-2);
\node[nd] (g) at (5.2,-2) {$u$};
\node[nd] (h) at (8.6,-2) {$v$};
\draw[blue] (g) to[bend left=26] node[lab,above] {add up to 5} (h);
\draw[undo] (h) to[bend left=26] node[lab,below] {cancel up to 2} (g);

\node[note,anchor=west] at (-.4,-3.4) {Blue increases input flow. Dashed orange decreases input flow.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Read the bottom row: the input flow is now `5 - 3 = 2`, so there is room
to add `7 - 2 = 5` units or to cancel the remaining `2`. These are amounts
we may change, not two additional flows already travelling through the graph.

A backward residual arrow is permission to cancel an earlier decision. It
need not be an arrow in the input. If the input also has `v -> u`, that input
edge gets its own pair; never combine it with this cancellation edge.

An **augmenting path** is a path from `s` to `t` using positive residual
capacities. Its bottleneck is the minimum residual capacity on the path.
Pushing that amount changes each input flow in the direction indicated by
the corresponding residual edge.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10cm}
```

## Trace the cancellation

For the six-vertex example, use residual path

```text
1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 2 -> 5 -> 6
```

The step `4 -> 2` cancels the old unit on input edge `2 -> 4`. All five
residual capacities on the path are `1`, so the bottleneck is `1`.


```{=latex}
% The residual path that repairs the first routing
\Needspace{6cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!40,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (2.6,1.3) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (2.6,-1.3) {3};
\node[nd] (c) at (5.2,1.3) {4};
\node[nd] (d) at (5.2,-1.3) {5};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (7.8,0) {6};

\draw[muted] (a)--node[lab]{1}(s);
\draw[blue] (s)--node[lab]{1}(b);
\draw[undo] (c)--node[lab]{1}(a);
\draw[blue] (a)--node[lab,pos=.65]{1}(d);
\draw[blue] (b)--node[lab,pos=.65]{1}(c);
\draw[muted] (t)--node[lab]{1}(c);
\draw[blue] (d)--node[lab]{1}(t);

\node[note,align=center] at (3.9,-2.5)
 {Positive residual capacities only. The chosen path is $1\to3\to4\to2\to5\to6$.\\
  Its orange step $4\to2$ cancels the old flow on input edge $2\to4$.\\
  Gray dashed arrows are other available cancellations, unused by this path.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```


Now apply the path as one revision: add one unit on its four blue input
edges, and remove the unit on `2 -> 4`. The resulting input flow is:


```{=latex}
% Input flows after repairing the first routing
\Needspace{6cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!40,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (2.6,1.3) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (2.6,-1.3) {3};
\node[nd] (c) at (5.2,1.3) {4};
\node[nd] (d) at (5.2,-1.3) {5};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (7.8,0) {6};

\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab]{1/1}(a);
\draw[blue] (s)--node[lab]{1/1}(b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab]{0/1}(c);
\draw[blue] (a)--node[lab,pos=.65]{1/1}(d);
\draw[blue] (b)--node[lab,pos=.65]{1/1}(c);
\draw[ar] (c)--node[lab]{1/1}(t);
\draw[blue] (d)--node[lab]{1/1}(t);

\node[note,align=center] at (3.9,-2.5)
 {Final input flows, labelled flow/capacity. Total delivered: 2.\\
  Edge $2\to4$ is unused; $1\to2$ and $4\to6$ keep their original unit.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```


Edges `1 -> 2` and `4 -> 6` keep their old unit. Read the final input flows:
they form the two routes promised above. We have not sent physical material
backward along an input road; we have replaced one feasible routing by another.

Why is an augmentation safe? The bottleneck protects every capacity bound.
At an internal path vertex, the two incident changes balance, whether a step
adds or cancels input flow. The source gains the bottleneck in net outgoing
flow and the sink gains the same amount in net incoming flow.

The minimum-cut proof later in this lesson will establish a stronger guarantee:
**whenever the current feasible flow is not maximum, its residual graph has
an augmenting path**. Thus the method can keep improving from any feasible
routing, including one obtained from an unfortunate early choice. Reverse
edges are what preserve this guarantee when earlier amounts need to move.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{9cm}
```

## Store paired edge IDs

The code needs to store the residual arrows we have just drawn. Whenever it
uses one arrow, it must also update that arrow's cancellation partner. Give
each residual arrow a unique **edge ID**, its index in a global array. One
input edge creates two stored entries.

### Create the pair before sending any flow

Start with vertices `0` and `1` and no edges. Adding the input edge
`0 -> 1` with capacity `7` creates:

- **ID 0**, from vertex 0 to vertex 1, with residual capacity 7: we may send
  up to 7 units on the input edge.
- **ID 1**, from vertex 1 to vertex 0, with residual capacity 0: we have sent
  nothing yet, so there is nothing to cancel.

These are two representations of what we may change on the **same input
edge**. Adding the reverse entry does not add a second input link.

```{=latex}
% Creating the first two residual entries
\Needspace{5cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[nd] (a) at (0,0) {0};
\node[nd] (b) at (3.8,0) {1};
\draw[blue] (a) to[bend left=28] node[lab,above] {ID 0: cap 7} (b);
\draw[undo] (b) to[bend left=28] node[lab,below] {ID 1: cap 0} (a);
\node[note,align=center] at (1.9,-1.7)
 {Circles: vertex numbers.\\Arrows: residual edge IDs.};
\node[note] at (6.7,1.2) {ID 0};
\node[note] at (8.8,1.2) {ID 1};
\node[note,anchor=east] at (5.7,.3) {to};
\node[note,anchor=east] at (5.7,-.7) {cap};
\node[cell] at (6.7,.3) {1};
\node[cell] at (8.8,.3) {0};
\node[cell,fill=blue!8] at (6.7,-.7) {7};
\node[cell,fill=orange!12] at (8.8,-.7) {0};
\node[note,align=center] at (7.75,-1.7)
 {Each column stores one entry.\\The reverse starts at zero.};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Each stored entry has a destination `to` and a remaining permission `cap`.
Thus `to[0] = 1`, `cap[0] = 7`, `to[1] = 0`, and `cap[1] = 0` initially.
The vertex numbers and the edge IDs are separate numbering systems.

For each vertex, `adj` lists the IDs of residual arrows leaving it:

```text
adj[0] = [0]    from vertex 0, examine residual entry 0
adj[1] = [1]    from vertex 1, examine residual entry 1
```

Store even the zero-capacity reverse entry. It will become usable after flow
is sent. A search follows an entry only when its current capacity is positive.

In the Python implementation, these fields are `self.to[id]` and
`self.cap[id]`. C++ stores them together as `edges[id].to` and `edges[id].cap`.
Below, `cap[id]` is shorthand for either language's residual capacity field.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12cm}
```

### Every push changes both entries

Send 5 units using ID 0. Its permission falls from 7 to 2, and the permission
to cancel that flow, ID 1, rises from 0 to 5. Later, cancelling 3 units means
using ID 1: its permission falls from 5 to 2, while ID 0 regains 3 units of
forward room.

```{=latex}
% Residual entries after adding and cancelling flow
\Needspace{8cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[note,anchor=west] at (-.4,2.8) {First send 5 units on ID 0. Input flow becomes 5.};
\node[nd] (a) at (0,1.3) {0};
\node[nd] (b) at (3.8,1.3) {1};
\draw[blue] (a) to[bend left=28] node[lab,above] {ID 0: cap 2} (b);
\draw[undo] (b) to[bend left=28] node[lab,below] {ID 1: cap 5} (a);
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4.5cm] at (5.4,1.3)
 {\texttt{cap[0] = 7 - 5 = 2}\\[4pt]
  \texttt{cap[1] = 0 + 5 = 5}};
\node[note,anchor=west] at (-.4,-.3) {Then cancel 3 units by using ID 1. Input flow becomes 2.};
\node[nd] (c) at (0,-1.8) {0};
\node[nd] (d) at (3.8,-1.8) {1};
\draw[blue] (c) to[bend left=28] node[lab,above] {ID 0: cap 5} (d);
\draw[undo] (d) to[bend left=28] node[lab,below] {ID 1: cap 2} (c);
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4.5cm] at (5.4,-1.8)
 {\texttt{cap[1] = 5 - 3 = 2}\\[4pt]
  \texttt{cap[0] = 2 + 3 = 5}};
\node[note,align=center] at (4.3,-3.4)
 {IDs and destinations never change. Only the two residual capacities change.};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

This is why the same two assignments work in either direction:

```text
cap[chosen ID]  -= amount
cap[partner ID] += amount
```

After the second row, the input edge carries `5 - 3 = 2` units. The two
residual capacities are `5` and `2`, whose sum remains the original capacity
`7`. The reverse member's capacity is exactly this input edge's current flow.

### Find the partner without searching

Create each pair consecutively, starting at ID zero:

```text
first input edge:   IDs 0 and 1
second input edge:  IDs 2 and 3
third input edge:   IDs 4 and 5
```

An even ID's partner is the next ID; an odd ID's partner is the previous ID.
In both C++ and Python, bitwise XOR with 1 performs exactly that exchange:

```text
0 ^ 1 = 1       1 ^ 1 = 0
2 ^ 1 = 3       3 ^ 1 = 2
4 ^ 1 = 5       5 ^ 1 = 4
```

```{=latex}
\Needspace{5cm}
```

Here `^` means **bitwise XOR**, not exponentiation. It toggles the last binary
bit, exchanging the two consecutive members of a pair. The update therefore
becomes:

```text
cap[edge]     -= delta
cap[edge ^ 1] += delta
```

For the cancellation above, `edge = 1`, so `edge ^ 1 = 0`: decrease the
backward permission and increase the forward permission. No special backward
case is needed. `add_edge` returns the even ID so callers can identify the
original input edge later.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12cm}
```

### Keep different input edges in different pairs

Continue the same example, where the first edge now carries 2 units. Add
another input edge `0 -> 1` with capacity 4, then an input edge `1 -> 0`
with capacity 6. They create two new pairs; they do not reuse the old pair.

```{=latex}
% Three input edges require three independent residual pairs
\Needspace{10cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[nd] (a) at (0,2.7) {0};
\node[nd] (b) at (3.8,2.7) {1};
\draw[blue] (a) to[bend left=28] node[lab,above] {ID 0: cap 5} (b);
\draw[undo] (b) to[bend left=28] node[lab,below] {ID 1: cap 2} (a);
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4.8cm] at (5.4,2.7)
 {Input edge A: $0\to1$.\\Capacity 7; current flow 2.};
\node[nd] (c) at (0,0) {0};
\node[nd] (d) at (3.8,0) {1};
\draw[blue] (c) to[bend left=28] node[lab,above] {ID 2: cap 4} (d);
\draw[undo] (d) to[bend left=28] node[lab,below] {ID 3: cap 0} (c);
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4.8cm] at (5.4,0)
 {Input edge B: $0\to1$.\\Capacity 4; current flow 0.};
\node[nd] (e) at (0,-2.7) {0};
\node[nd] (f) at (3.8,-2.7) {1};
\draw[undo] (e) to[bend left=28] node[lab,above] {ID 5: cap 0} (f);
\draw[blue] (f) to[bend left=28] node[lab,below] {ID 4: cap 6} (e);
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4.8cm] at (5.4,-2.7)
 {Input edge C: $1\to0$.\\Capacity 6; current flow 0.};
\node[note,align=center] at (4.6,-4.2)
 {Each row shows a separate pair between the same two vertices.\\
  ID 1 cancels edge A's flow; ID 4 adds flow on edge C.};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

In particular, IDs 1 and 4 both point from vertex 1 to vertex 0, but they
have different meanings. Using ID 1 reduces flow on input edge A; using ID 4
increases flow on input edge C. Their partner IDs are 0 and 5 respectively.
Knowing only the destination vertex would not tell us which partner to update.

The outgoing lists now contain:

```text
adj[0] = [0, 2, 5]
adj[1] = [1, 3, 4]
```

An outgoing list contains **edge IDs**, not destination vertices. Its local
positions are different from those IDs: position 1 of `adj[0]` contains edge
ID 2, and `to[2]` tells us that this edge leads to vertex 1. Later, Dinic's
current pointer will remember a position in such a list.

# Dinic: organize the searches into phases

Residual paths let us repair earlier choices, but correctness alone does
not guarantee speed. Even with integer capacities, a poor choice of paths
can make progress depend on the amount of flow rather than the graph size.

Consider this network. All four outer edges have capacity `U`; the central
edge has capacity 1. Take `U = 1 000 000 000`:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={font=\small,align=left}]
\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {$s$};
\node[nd] (a) at (3,1.2) {$a$};
\node[nd] (b) at (3,-1.2) {$b$};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (6,0) {$t$};
\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab]{$U$}(a);
\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab]{$U$}(b);
\draw[->,very thick,red!70!black] (a)--node[lab]{1}(b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab]{$U$}(t);
\draw[ar] (b)--node[lab]{$U$}(t);
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4.4cm] at (7.1,0)
 {Input capacities.\\[4pt]
  Maximum flow: $2U$.\\
  Send $U$ on each outer branch.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

**Arbitrary paths can alternate between using and cancelling the central
edge.** Starting from zero, choose:

1. `s -> a -> b -> t`: send 1, limited by `a -> b`.
2. `s -> b -> a -> t`: send 1, using the residual arrow `b -> a` to cancel
   the unit on `a -> b`.

After these two augmentations, each outer input edge carries 1, while the
central edge again carries zero. The total value is 2. Repeat the same
pair of choices: each pair adds only 2, and restores the central edge to
zero flow. After `k` pairs, every outer edge carries `k` and the value is
`2k`. Both choices remain possible until `k = U`.

This legal execution needs **`2U` augmentations to obtain value `2U`**:
two billion augmentations on a graph with only four vertices and five edges.
The total always increases, so the algorithm terminates, but far too slowly.

**Dinic uses shortest-path levels to avoid this execution.** The first BFS
assigns `level[s] = 0`, `level[a] = level[b] = 1`, and `level[t] = 2`.
During a phase, flow searches may follow only arrows that advance exactly
one level. The central arrow `a -> b` stays at level 1, so it is excluded.
Dinic sends `U` on `s -> a -> t` and `U` on `s -> b -> t`: **two
augmentations in one phase** reach the maximum.

This example exposes the danger of arbitrary paths; other algorithms, such
as Edmonds-Karp, also avoid it by choosing shortest residual paths. Dinic
goes further: it works through the current shortest-path levels until no
allowed source-to-sink path remains, then recomputes the levels. We will
show that this organization bounds the number of phases by `O(V)`,
independently of the capacity values.

```{=latex}
\newpage
```

Dinic has two nested loops. The **outer loop** runs BFS on the full residual
graph. If the sink is reachable, the **inner loop** sends flow using just the
current levels. When that inner loop is blocked, the outer loop runs a fresh
BFS and may discover longer routes. The algorithm returns the maximum value
only when a full BFS cannot reach the sink.

```{=latex}
% The outer Dinic loop continues after each blocking phase
\Needspace{9cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 box/.style={draw,rounded corners,align=center,text width=4cm,
             inner sep=5pt,font=\small,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick},lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small}]
\node[box] (start) at (0,3.2) {Start with flow value 0.};
\node[box] (bfs) at (0,1.7) {Run BFS on all positive residual arrows.};
\node[box] (test) at (0,.2) {Does BFS reach the sink?};
\node[box,fill=green!12,text width=3.5cm] (done) at (5.2,.2)
 {Return the accumulated value.\\It is the maximum flow.};
\node[box,fill=blue!7] (phase) at (0,-2)
 {One phase: keep these levels fixed.\\
  Send allowed paths until blocked.\\
  Add the amount sent to the total.};
\draw[ar] (start)--(bfs);
\draw[ar] (bfs)--(test);
\draw[ar] (test)--node[lab,above]{No}(done);
\draw[ar] (test)--node[lab,right]{Yes}(phase);
\draw[ar,blue!65!black] (phase.west)--(-3.4,-2)--(-3.4,1.7)--(bfs.west);
\node[align=center,text width=2cm,font=\small,anchor=east] at (-3.6,-.2)
 {New phase:\\recompute levels};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

```{=latex}
\Needspace{11cm}
```

## Build a level graph with BFS

```{=latex}
% The first BFS level graph
\Needspace{7cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!40,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (3,1.2) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (3,-1.2) {3};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (6,0) {4};
\draw[blue] (s)--node[lab] {3} (a);
\draw[blue] (s)--node[lab] {2} (b);
\draw[muted] (a)--node[lab] {1} (b);
\draw[blue] (a)--node[lab] {2} (t);
\draw[blue] (b)--node[lab] {4} (t);
\node[note] at (0,-.85) {level 0};
\node[note] at (3,2) {level 1};
\node[note] at (3,-2) {level 1};
\node[note] at (6,-.85) {level 2};
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4.2cm] at (7.1,0)
 {Count arrows from vertex 1.\\[5pt]
  Vertices 2 and 3 need one step.\\
  Vertex 4 needs two steps.};

\node[note,align=center] at (3,-2.8) {Initial residual capacities; no flow has been sent yet.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

`level` is an array with one entry per vertex. **`level[v]` is the smallest
number of usable residual arrows needed to reach vertex `v` from the source.**
Usable means positive residual capacity. Each arrow counts as one step,
regardless of its capacity; the level is a distance, not an amount of flow.

In the opening network, before sending flow, the source is vertex 1:

```text
level[1] = 0    already at the source: no arrow needed
level[2] = 1    follow 1 -> 2
level[3] = 1    follow 1 -> 3
level[4] = 2    follow 1 -> 2 -> 4, or 1 -> 3 -> 4
```

"Set `level[4]` to 2" means storing `2` in vertex 4's array entry. The longer
route `1 -> 2 -> 3` does not change `level[3]`: the direct route needs only
one step.

BFS computes these distances one layer at a time:

1. Initialize levels to `-1` (not reached), set `level[s] = 0`, and enqueue `s`.
2. Pop a vertex `u`. Inspect all its positive-capacity residual arrows,
   including cancellation arrows.
3. For each destination `v` still at `-1`, assign `level[v] = level[u] + 1`
   and enqueue it. Keep an already assigned level: the first discovery is shortest.
4. Repeat until the queue is empty. Vertices still at `-1` are unreachable.

If `level[t] == -1`, no augmenting path exists and the algorithm stops.
Otherwise, this phase's flow searches use only arrows advancing one layer,
`level[v] == level[u] + 1`. These arrows form the **level graph**. Since
`v = to[edge]`, the code condition is:

```text
cap[edge] > 0 and level[to[edge]] == level[u] + 1
```

In the drawing above, blue arrows advance one layer. Vertices 2 and 3 both
have level 1, so their dashed connecting arrow is excluded from the level
graph. Arrow labels are residual capacities; vertex "level" labels are
distances. Levels strictly increase along retained arrows, preventing cycles.





```{=latex}
\newpage
```

## One phase: send a blocking flow

We are now inside **one iteration of Dinic's outer loop**. Keep the current
BFS levels fixed, repeatedly find an allowed source-to-sink path, and send
its bottleneck. Eventually no path remains that advances through these fixed
levels. The extra flow sent during this phase is called a **blocking flow**:
every source-to-sink path in the phase's initial level graph now has an edge
with zero residual capacity.

**This ends the phase, not the algorithm.** Keep the flow already sent and
run BFS again on the full updated residual graph, including arrows excluded
during the phase that just ended. That BFS can reveal a longer route and start another phase.
Only when this full BFS cannot reach the sink is the accumulated flow maximum.

For the opening network, first send 2 along `1 -> 2 -> 4`, then 2 along
`1 -> 3 -> 4`. In these levels, `2 -> 3` is forbidden, so the phase stops
at value 4:


```{=latex}

 {Phase 1 adds $2+2=4$.\\[5pt]
  Both two-edge routes are blocked.\\

\node[note,align=center] at (3,-2.8) {Flow/capacity after phase 1. Levels are fixed for the whole phase.};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

The first phase was blocking but not globally maximum. Rebuilding levels
revealed the extra route; the final failed BFS certifies that none remains.

```{=latex}
  Blue and orange form $1\to3\to4\to2\to5\to6$.\\
  Gray arrows are available cancellations that do not advance one BFS level.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

The original input edge is `2 -> 4`. Its orange cancellation arrow is
`4 -> 2`: backward relative to that input edge, but from level 2 to level 3
in this new BFS. It therefore satisfies `level[to] == level[u] + 1`, just
like the blue arrows. Gray arrows `2 -> 1` and `6 -> 4` go to smaller levels,
so this phase excludes them. The highlighted path adds one unit, raising the
total from 1 to 2.

```{=latex}

```

## Current pointers and the explicit search stack

Use this small network throughout the subsection. Vertices are 0-based, as
in the implementation. The BFS levels are already computed and remain fixed:

```{=latex}
% The four-vertex search example used throughout section 3.3
\Needspace{7cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,

 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},

 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!40,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=16mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {0};
\node[nd] (u) at (2.7,0) {1};
\node[nd] (dead) at (5.4,1.2) {2};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (5.4,-1.2) {3};

\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab,above]{ID 0: 4}(u);
\draw[ar] (u)--node[lab,above]{ID 2: 3}(dead);
\draw[ar] (u)--node[lab,below]{ID 4: 2}(t);
\node[note] at (0,-.8) {level 0};
\node[note] at (2.7,-.8) {level 1};
\node[note] at (5.4,2) {level 2};
\node[note] at (5.4,-2) {level 2};
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4cm] at (6.6,0)
 {Source: 0. Sink: 3.\\[4pt]
  Vertex 2 is a dead end.\\
  The other branch reaches the sink.};
\node[note,align=center] at (3.8,-2.9)
 {Arrow labels are residual edge ID: capacity. Zero-capacity reverse entries are omitted.};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

### First understand the search, without the arrays

We need a complete route from source 0 to sink 3. Start by trying `0 -> 1`,
then `1 -> 2`. Vertex 2 has no allowed continuation, so this attempt fails.
Return to vertex 1 and try its other branch, `1 -> 3`. That reaches the sink.

**Exploring an arrow does not send flow yet.** We change capacities only after
finding a complete source-to-sink route. Returning from the dead end abandons
a search attempt; there is no flow on that branch to cancel.

### Remember which outgoing entry to try next

The residual pairs were inserted in this order:

```text
input 0 -> 1: forward ID 0, reverse ID 1
input 1 -> 2: forward ID 2, reverse ID 3
input 1 -> 3: forward ID 4, reverse ID 5
```

Thus vertex 1's outgoing list is `adj[1] = [1, 2, 4]`. The variable `ptr[1]`
is a bookmark: **the position in this list where its search should resume**.

Initially `ptr[1] = 0`, selecting ID 1. This reverse entry has capacity zero,
so skip it. Position 1 selects ID 2, which leads to the dead end. Once that
attempt fails, advance to position 2, selecting ID 4:

```{=latex}
% The current pointer chooses a position in the outgoing list
\Needspace{6cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!40,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=16mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[note,anchor=east] at (-1.2,0) {adj[1]};
\node[note] at (0,1) {position 0};
\node[note] at (3,1) {position 1};
\node[note] at (6,1) {position 2};
\node[cell,fill=black!5] at (0,0) {ID 1};
\node[cell,fill=black!5] at (3,0) {ID 2};
\node[cell,fill=blue!8] at (6,0) {ID 4};
\node[note,align=center] at (0,-1.1) {to vertex 0\\cap 0: skip};
\node[note,align=center] at (3,-1.1) {to vertex 2\\tried; dead end};
\node[note,align=center] at (6,-1.1) {to vertex 3\\next choice};
\draw[blue] (3,-2.1)--node[lab,below]{ptr[1]: 1 to 2}(6,-2.1);
\node[note,align=center] at (2.5,-3.1)
 {After the dead end, ptr[1] = 2 selects edge ID 4, not edge ID 2.};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

In general, `edge = adj[u][ptr[u]]` reads the selected edge ID, then
`v = to[edge]` reads its destination. These are three separate quantities:
list position, edge ID, and destination vertex.

### Store the route currently being explored

The iterative search keeps three lists, used as stacks: append to extend the
route; remove the last entry to return one step.

- `vertices` lists the visited vertices on the current candidate route.
  Its last entry tells us where the search is now.
- `path` lists the residual edge IDs joining those vertices. We need the
  exact IDs to update their capacities and their paired reverse entries.
- `bottleneck` records the minimum capacity along each prefix of that route.
  Keeping every prefix value lets us recover the previous minimum when we
  remove the last step.

Start with `vertices = [0]`, `path = []`, and `bottleneck = [4]`. The initial
4 is a safe upper bound: only 4 units can leave the source. After edge ID 0,
the minimum is still 4; after edge ID 2, it becomes `min(4,3) = 3`:

```{=latex}

\Needspace{6cm}

\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,

\node[note,anchor=west] at (-.4,2.4) {A. Search reaches vertex 2, but no continuation reaches the sink.};

\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {0};
\node[nd] (u) at (2.7,0) {1};
\node[nd] (dead) at (5.4,1.2) {2};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (5.4,-1.2) {3};
\draw[blue] (s)--node[lab,above]{ID 0: 4} (u);
\draw[blue] (u)--node[lab,above]{ID 2: 3} (dead);
\draw[ar] (u)--node[lab,below]{ID 4: 2} (t);
\node[note,anchor=west] at (6.6,0) {\texttt{vertices = [0, 1, 2]}\\[4pt]
\texttt{path = [0, 2]}\\[4pt]
\texttt{bottleneck = [4, 4, 3]}\\[4pt]
\texttt{ptr[1] = 1}};
\node[note,align=center] at (5,-2.4) {The path is only a candidate. No flow has been sent; all capacities are unchanged.};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Return to vertex 1: remove vertex 2, the last edge ID 2, and its prefix
bottleneck 3. Advance `ptr[1]` from position 1 to position 2:

```{=latex}

\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {0};
\node[nd] (u) at (2.7,0) {1};
\node[nd] (dead) at (5.4,1.2) {2};
```

Position 2 of `adj[1]` contains ID 4. Follow it to the sink, append vertex
3 and edge ID 4, and append `min(4,2) = 2` to the bottleneck list:

```{=latex}

\Needspace{6cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
```

At the sink, read the last bottleneck and update every edge ID in `path`
together with its reverse. Here ID 0's capacity becomes `4 - 2 = 2`, and
ID 4's becomes `2 - 2 = 0`; reverse IDs 1 and 5 each gain 2. The unused
branch through vertex 2 still carries no flow.


### After sending flow: a new search in the same phase

Continue with the same four-vertex graph. We have just sent 2 units on
`0 -> 1 -> 3`. The drawing below shows the residual capacities afterwards:

```{=latex}
% The same four-vertex graph after sending two units
\Needspace{8cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,

 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},

 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!45,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {0};
\node[nd] (u) at (3.5,0) {1};
\node[nd] (dead) at (7,1.5) {2};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (7,-1.5) {3};
\draw[blue] (s) to[bend left=23] node[lab,above]{ID 0: 2}(u);
\draw[undo] (u) to[bend left=23] node[lab,below]{ID 1: 2}(s);
\draw[ar] (u)--node[lab,above]{ID 2: 3}(dead);
\draw[muted] (u) to[bend left=13] node[lab,above]{ID 4: 0}(t);
\draw[undo] (t) to[bend left=23] node[lab,below]{ID 5: 2}(u);
\node[note] at (0,.9) {level 0};
\node[note] at (3.5,.9) {level 1};
\node[note] at (7,2.3) {level 2};
\node[note] at (7,-2.3) {level 2};
\node[note,align=center] at (3.5,-3.2)
 {Current total: 2. Labels are edge ID: remaining residual capacity.\\
  ID 4 is now empty. Reverse IDs 1 and 5 have capacity, but go to smaller levels.\\
  The zero-capacity reverse ID 3 is omitted.};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Three kinds of state have different lifetimes:

- **Capacities and the accumulated total stay.** They describe the flow
  already sent. The total is 2.
- **Current pointers stay for this phase.** In particular, `ptr[0] = 0` and
  `ptr[1] = 2`. Vertex 1 has already discarded its first two outgoing entries.
- **The candidate route starts over.** A new search creates `vertices = [0]`,
  `path = []`, and `bottleneck = [4]`, using the same safe bound as before.

Keeping a pointer does not mean keeping the old route. It means remembering
which outgoing entries have already failed under these fixed levels.

**We could reset the pointers after every completed path and still obtain
the correct answer.** However, we would repeat searches already known to fail.
Keeping the pointers avoids this repeated work.

The reason this is safe is that **an impasse stays an impasse within the same
phase**. The levels are fixed, and the residual capacities of arrows advancing
one level can only decrease. Sending flow creates cancellation permissions
in the opposite direction, towards smaller levels in this phase; these new permissions
are not allowed in this phase. Thus no new allowed continuation can appear
behind an entry we have already discarded.

In our example, `adj[1] = [1,2,4]` and `ptr[1] = 2`. We already know that
ID 1 goes to a smaller level and ID 2 leads to the dead end at vertex 2.
Resetting `ptr[1]` to zero would merely check these two entries again.

**Keeping a pointer does not skip an edge that is still useful.** After the
successful push, `ptr[0]` is still zero, selecting ID 0, which still has
capacity 2. The next search will try it again, as we now follow step by step.

**Follow the next search.**

1. At vertex 0, position `ptr[0] = 0` selects ID 0. It still has capacity 2
   and advances from level 0 to level 1, so follow it to vertex 1.
2. At vertex 1, resume at position `ptr[1] = 2`, selecting ID 4. Its capacity
   is now zero, so advance `ptr[1]` to 3. But `adj[1] = [1,2,4]` has only
   positions 0, 1, and 2: position 3 is past the end. No entry remains.
3. Return from vertex 1 to vertex 0, removing vertex 1 and ID 0 from the
   candidate route. Advance `ptr[0]` to 1. ID 0 still has capacity, but its
   destination has no allowed way onward, so this branch cannot reach the sink.
4. `adj[0] = [0]` has only position 0. The source's pointer is now past its
   end too. The candidate route empties and this search returns 0.

```{=latex}
% Current pointers reach the ends of their outgoing lists
\Needspace{8cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,

 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!45,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[note,anchor=east] at (-1.2,1) {adj[1]};
\node[cell] at (0,1) {ID 1};
\node[cell] at (2,1) {ID 2};
\node[cell,fill=black!5] (a) at (4,1) {ID 4};
\node[cell,dashed] (b) at (6,1) {end};
\node[note] at (4,1.9) {position 2};
\node[note] at (6,1.9) {position 3};
\draw[blue] (a.south) to[bend right=30] node[lab,below]{ptr[1]: 2 to 3}(b.south);
\node[note,anchor=east] at (-1.2,-1.9) {adj[0]};
\node[cell] (c) at (0,-1.9) {ID 0};
\node[cell,dashed] (d) at (2,-1.9) {end};
\node[note] at (0,-1) {position 0};
\node[note] at (2,-1) {position 1};
\draw[blue] (c.south) to[bend right=30] node[lab,below]{ptr[0]: 0 to 1}(d.south);
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4cm] at (3.8,-1.9)
 {ID 0 still has capacity 2.\\Its destination has no allowed continuation, so skip this branch.};
\node[note,align=center] at (2.6,-3.5)
 {The dashed end boxes are past the lists, not stored edges.\\
  ptr[1] = len(adj[1]) and ptr[0] = len(adj[0]) mean there is no entry left to try.};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

**Returning 0 here means no additional flow was found.** It does not erase
the 2 units already sent. The inner loop ends because no route remains in
these levels; Dinic then runs a new BFS on the updated residual graph.

On this particular graph, the new BFS reaches vertices 0, 1, and 2, but not
sink 3. The algorithm therefore stops and returns the accumulated value 2.
There is no further phase in this example.

**If the new BFS does reach the sink on another instance**, begin a new phase:
keep the capacities and total, but reset all current pointers to zero. Entries
rejected in the preceding phase may now belong to a new allowed route. The
candidate-route lists also start over as usual.

Resetting at a new phase is therefore different from resetting after every
path: new levels can change which directions are allowed. Pointer reuse
within a phase saves work without ruling out a valid route; the efficiency
discussion below explains how this gives the running-time bound. The explicit lists
carry out the exploration and backtracking without recursive calls.

```{=latex}
\newpage
```

## Why Dinic returns a maximum flow

The running-time bound alone does not prove that the answer is optimal.
Correctness needs three facts: the current flow stays valid, a blocked phase
cannot cause a premature return, and the final failed BFS certifies optimality.

### Each augmentation preserves a valid flow and its reported value

The initial zero flow satisfies capacities and conservation. On a residual
source-to-sink path, send its bottleneck `delta`. A forward residual step adds
to its input edge's flow; a backward step subtracts from it. The bottleneck
ensures that neither change crosses a capacity bound or makes an input flow
negative.

At every internal path vertex, the two incident changes balance: the net
change in incoming minus outgoing flow is zero, including when a step cancels
an earlier assignment. The source supplies `delta` more in net flow, and the
sink absorbs `delta` more. Thus the resulting assignment is feasible, and
adding `delta` to the stored total gives its actual flow value.

### Restricting one phase to its levels does not discard future routes

The restriction is temporary. Dinic retains the full residual graph; it only
limits which arrows a path search may use during this phase.

If BFS reaches the sink, a shortest residual route exists. Every arrow of
that route advances one BFS level, so the new level graph contains a usable
source-to-sink path. With current pointers reset, the search can find an
augmentation; it is not prevented from starting by the level restriction.

After a blocking flow, the inner search returns zero. Dinic does **not**
return the accumulated total yet: BFS again examines all positive residual
arrows, without using the old current pointers to skip entries. It may find
a longer route or one using a cancellation arrow. If so, reset the pointers
and begin another phase. Only a failed BFS of the full residual graph ends
the algorithm.

```{=latex}
\newpage
```

### A failed full BFS proves that no larger feasible flow exists

Run BFS from the source using **all positive residual arrows**, including
cancellation arrows. Suppose it cannot reach the sink. Let `S` contain every
vertex it did reach, not just the source. The sink lies outside `S`.

The following network has a feasible flow of 5. Labels show input
flow/capacity. The shaded region will be the set reached by the final BFS:

```{=latex}
\draw[ar] (t) to[bend left=18] node[lab]{3}(c);
\draw[ar] (d) to[bend left=18] node[lab]{1}(t);
\draw[ar] (t) to[bend left=18] node[lab]{2}(d);
\node at (1,2.1) {BFS reaches $s,a,b$};
\node at (5.8,2.1) {$c,d,t$ remain unreachable};
\node[font=\small] at (3.5,-2.2) {Residual capacities. No positive arrow leaves the shaded region.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

BFS reaches `a` and `b` from `s`, but has no residual arrow out of the shaded
region. Arrows such as `c -> a` point **into** it, so they cannot help the
search leave it. Why does this failure prove that 5 is optimal?

```{=latex}
\newpage
```

**First, every input edge leaving `S` must be full.** Here `a -> c` carries
3 out of 3, and `b -> d` carries 2 out of 2. If either had spare capacity,
BFS could cross to its outside endpoint. In general:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small}]
\fill[blue!6,rounded corners] (-.7,-.7) rectangle (.7,.7);
\node[nd] (u) at (0,0) {$u$};
\node[nd] (v) at (4.5,0) {$v$};
\draw[->,thick] (u)--node[lab,above]{input flow $f$, capacity $c$}(v);
\node[font=\small] at (0,-1) {Inside $S$};
\node[font=\small] at (4.5,-1) {Outside $S$};
\node[align=left,text width=6cm,font=\small,anchor=west] at (6,0)
 {Spare capacity $c-f>0$ would let BFS leave $S$.\\[4pt]
  Since it cannot leave: $c-f=0$, so $f=c$.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

**Second, every input edge entering `S` must carry zero flow.** This also
matters: flow coming back into `S` would reduce its net delivery. In our
example, the entering input edge `c -> b` carries zero. If it carried a
positive amount, its cancellation arrow `b -> c` would let BFS leave `S`:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small}]
\fill[blue!6,rounded corners] (-.7,-.7) rectangle (.7,.7);
\node[nd] (u) at (0,0) {$u$};
\node[nd] (v) at (4.5,0) {$v$};
\draw[->,thick] (v) to[bend right=23] node[lab,above]{input flow $f$}(u);
\draw[->,thick,dashed,orange!75!black] (u) to[bend right=23]
 node[lab,below]{cancellation capacity $f$}(v);
\node[font=\small] at (0,-1.3) {Inside $S$};
\node[font=\small] at (4.5,-1.3) {Outside $S$};
\node[align=left,text width=6cm,font=\small,anchor=west] at (6,0)
 {If $f>0$, the orange residual arrow would let BFS leave $S$.\\[4pt]
  Since it cannot leave: $f=0$.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

**Finally, compare our delivery with the best any flow could deliver.**
Add conservation over all vertices of `S` except the source. Internal
transfers cancel: a unit sent from `s` to `a`, for instance, stays within
`S`. Only transfers across its boundary count towards the net delivery:

```text
flow value = flow leaving S - flow entering S
```

In the example, the current value is `3 + 2 - 0 = 5`. No feasible flow can
have a larger value: the only input edges leaving `S` have total capacity
`3 + 2 = 5`. Reorganizing the flow inside either region cannot increase
these capacities, and sending flow back into `S` can only reduce net delivery.

In general, let `C` be the sum of the input capacities leaving `S`.
The two facts above give:

```text
Our current flow:  value = C - 0 = C
Any feasible flow: value <= C
```

Our feasible flow attains an upper bound valid for every feasible flow, so
it is maximum. This is why a failed BFS of the full residual graph is a
certificate of optimality, rather than just a failed local search.
The next subsection proves that Dinic reaches this condition in finitely
many phases. Chapter 4 develops this boundary argument as a minimum cut.

```{=latex}
\newpage
```

## Why Dinic finishes efficiently

There are two separate questions: how many phases can occur, and how much
work one phase can do. Write `V` for the number of vertices and `E` for the
number of input edges. The representation stores `2E` residual entries;
that factor of two does not change an asymptotic bound.

### Each successful phase makes the shortest remaining route longer

Consider this four-vertex network, starting with zero flow. The numbers
on the arrows are input capacities. BFS assigns levels 0, 1, 1, and 2:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,

 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={font=\small,align=left}]
\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (3,1.2) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (3,-1.2) {3};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (6,0) {4};
\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab]{3}(a);
\draw[ar] (s)--node[lab]{2}(b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab]{1}(b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab]{2}(t);
\draw[ar] (b)--node[lab]{4}(t);
\node[note] at (0,-.85) {level 0};
\node[note] at (3,2) {level 1};
\node[note] at (3,-2) {level 1};
\node[note] at (6,-.85) {level 2};
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4.4cm] at (7.1,0)

  Source: vertex 1.\\
  Sink: vertex 4.\\
  Flow value: 0.\\

\node[note] at (3,-2.7) {Input capacities before any flow is sent.};

```

In phase 1, send 2 units along `1 -> 2 -> 4`, then 2 units along
`1 -> 3 -> 4`. The total flow becomes 4. The arrows `2 -> 4` and `1 -> 3`
now have zero forward residual capacity, blocking both two-arrow routes.

The drawing below shows the forward residual capacities after these two
pushes, keeping **the same levels as above**. The route `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4`
still has capacity, but its middle arrow stays at level 1, so the phase's
flow search cannot use it:

```{=latex}
% The next route is longer after the two short routes are blocked
\Needspace{7cm}

\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (3,1.2) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (3,-1.2) {3};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (6,0) {4};

\draw[muted] (s)--node[lab]{0}(b);
\draw[->,very thick,draw=red!70!black] (a)--node[lab]{1}(b);
\draw[muted] (a)--node[lab]{0}(t);
\draw[blue] (b)--node[lab]{2}(t);

  At phase start: shortest routes have 2 arrows.\\
  Blue: advances one level.\\
  Red: same level, forbidden in this phase.};
\node[note,align=center] at (3,-3)
 {Forward residual capacities after phase 1. Positive reverse arrows are omitted here.\\
  The residual route has levels $0,1,1,2$. Its red arrow prevents using it in this phase.};
```

Route `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4` takes three steps. Using the levels computed for
this phase, its level sequence is `0,1,1,2`: crossing `2 -> 3` uses a step
without increasing the level. **The flow search does not take this route in
phase 1.**

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10cm}
```

After phase 1 ends, run BFS again on the full residual graph. It assigns
levels 0, 1, 2, and 3 to vertices 1, 2, 3, and 4 respectively:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},

\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (3,1.2) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (3,-1.2) {3};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (6,0) {4};
\draw[allowed] (s) to[bend left=18] node[lab]{1}(a);
\draw[other] (a) to[bend left=18] node[lab]{2}(s);
\draw[other] (b)--node[lab]{2}(s);
\draw[allowed] (a)--node[lab]{1}(b);
\draw[other] (t)--node[lab]{2}(a);
\draw[allowed] (b) to[bend left=18] node[lab]{2}(t);
\draw[other] (t) to[bend left=18] node[lab]{2}(b);
\node[note] at (0,-.85) {level 0};
\node[note] at (3,2.15) {level 1};
\node[note] at (3,-2.15) {level 2};
\node[note] at (6,-.85) {level 3};
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4.4cm] at (7.1,0)
 {Start of phase 2.\\[4pt]
  Flow value: still 4.\\
  New shortest distance: 3.\\[4pt]
  Blue: allowed in phase 2.\\
  Gray: goes to a smaller level.};
\node[note,align=center] at (3,-2.9)
 {All positive residual arrows, with the new BFS levels.\\
  Residual capacities have not changed: BFS only recomputed the levels.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

The middle arrow `2 -> 3` now goes from level 1 to level 2. The whole blue
route `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4` advances one level at every step, so phase 2 can
send its bottleneck of 1. The sink's shortest distance has increased from
2 to 3 between the starts of the two phases.

To understand why this always happens, keep the BFS numbers from the start
of the phase written beside the vertices, even after capacities change.
Call these fixed numbers `L[v]`. The source has `L[s] = 0` and the sink has
`L[t] = D`. We will compare routes using these same numbers; we are not
running a new BFS yet.

**Before the phase, one residual arrow can increase `L` by at most 1.**
For example, suppose BFS assigns `L[u] = 2`. If a positive residual arrow
`u -> v` exists, we can reach `v` in at most three steps: take a shortest
two-step route to `u`, then that arrow. Thus BFS cannot assign `L[v] = 5`;
it must assign `L[v] <= 3`. In general:

```text
L[v] <= L[u] + 1
```

An arrow may go to the next level (`L[v] = L[u] + 1`), stay at the same
level, or go to a smaller level. It cannot increase the level by more than 1.

This describes the **full residual graph**. The **flow search during this
phase** follows only positive-capacity arrows satisfying `L[v] = L[u] + 1`.
It cannot follow an arrow to the same level or to a smaller level, even if
that arrow has positive residual capacity. The levels remain fixed throughout
the phase; the next BFS will examine all positive residual arrows again.

**Changing capacities during the phase preserves this limit.** Arrows that
remain usable already satisfied it. An arrow that becomes usable because
we sent flow is the reverse of an arrow used by this phase. We only sent
flow from a level `d` to level `d+1`, so the newly available reverse goes
from `d+1` to `d`. It also cannot skip forward over a level:

```{=latex}
% A new reverse arrow goes backward through this phase's levels
\Needspace{6cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!45,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[nd] (a) at (0,0) {$u$};
\node[nd] (b) at (4.6,0) {$v$};
\draw[blue] (a) to[bend left=27] node[lab,above]{used during this phase}(b);
\draw[undo] (b) to[bend left=27] node[lab,below]{new cancellation permission}(a);
\node[note] at (0,-1.3) {level $d$};
\node[note] at (4.6,-1.3) {level $d+1$};
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4.8cm] at (6,0)
 {Sending flow forward makes its reverse available.\\[4pt]
  The reverse decreases the level by 1, so this phase cannot use it.};
\node[note,align=center] at (4,-2.5)
 {These are the levels computed by BFS for this phase. A later BFS may assign different ones.};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

**Now ask whether a route of `D` arrows could remain after the phase.**
It would have to start at level 0 and finish at level `D`. Since each arrow
increases the level by at most 1, it would have to increase it by exactly 1
on every step. There is no spare step for moving sideways or backward.

For instance, with `D = 3`, compare these sequences of fixed level numbers:

```{=latex}
\Needspace{4cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 n/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=7mm,fill=white,font=\small},
 note/.style={anchor=west,font=\small}]
\foreach \x/\v in {0/0,1/1,2/2,3/3}
  \node[n] (a\x) at (1.3*\x,0) {\v};
\foreach \x/\y in {0/1,1/2,2/3}
  \draw[->,thick,blue!65!black] (a\x)--(a\y);
\node[note] at (6,0) {3 arrows: every step increases the level.};
\foreach \x/\v in {0/0,1/1,2/1,3/2,4/3}
  \node[n] (b\x) at (1.3*\x,-1.1) {\v};
\foreach \x/\y in {0/1,1/2,2/3,3/4}
  \draw[->,thick] (b\x)--(b\y);
\node[note] at (6,-1.1) {4 arrows: one step stays at level 1.};
\node[font=\small] at (5,-2)
  {The circles show fixed BFS levels, not vertex IDs.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

But the phase stopped precisely because **no positive-capacity source-to-sink
route increasing the level at every step remained**. That is the definition
of its blocking flow. So a route of `D` arrows cannot remain. A shorter one
is also impossible: fewer than `D` increases of at most 1 cannot take us from
0 to `D`.

Consequently, any remaining route needs **more than `D` arrows**. Here is
how this limits the number of phases.

**Each new phase needs a larger sink distance.** At the start of a phase,
BFS finds the shortest residual source-to-sink route; let its length be `D`.
After that phase, no route of length `D` or less remains. The next BFS
therefore either fails, ending the algorithm, or finds a distance of at
least `D+1`. In the latter case, we begin another phase. Thus the distances
at the starts of successive phases are strictly increasing integers.

**A finite shortest distance cannot exceed `V-1`.** If a route visits a
vertex twice, the part between those two visits is a cycle. Removing that
part gives a shorter route with the same source and sink. So a shortest
route never repeats a vertex: it visits at most `V` vertices and uses at
most `V-1` arrows. This remains true when some arrows cancel earlier flow.

For example, suppose the graph has `V = 6` vertices and the first BFS finds
the sink at distance 2. The distances at the starts of later phases can
only come from this list, in order:

```text
Possible phase-start distances:  2, 3, 4, 5
An execution might use:          2,    4, 5, then no route
```

Some distances may be skipped, but none can be repeated. Distance 6 cannot
occur: a shortest route of six arrows would need seven distinct vertices,
and this graph has only six. After a phase starting at distance 5, the next
BFS must therefore fail.

In general, the possible distances are the `V-1` integers from 1 to `V-1`
(the source and sink are distinct). Each phase uses a different one, so
there are at most `V-1` phases, followed by one final unsuccessful BFS.
This gives `O(V)` phases. We are counting whole blocking-flow phases here;
one phase may send flow along several routes.

### Bound the work inside one phase

**Failed entries are not retried indefinitely.** Each `ptr[u]` only advances
through `adj[u]`; it never moves backward during a phase. Across all vertices,
there are `2E` entries to pass. Hence these advances and the dead branches
they discard account for `O(E)` work.

**Every successful push uses up at least one allowed edge.** We send the
path's minimum residual capacity, so some edge on that path becomes empty.
It stays empty for this phase: restoring its capacity would require using
its reverse, which decreases the level and is forbidden in this phase. There are only
`2E` residual entries, so there are at most `O(E)` successful pushes.

**One successful route has at most `V-1` arrows.** Following and updating its
path stacks costs `O(V)`. Several routes may share an edge that still has
room; that repeated productive work is included in this `O(V)` per push.
Together with the failed-entry work, one blocking phase costs `O(VE)`.

```{=latex}
% Multiply the two bounds to obtain Dinic general running time
\Needspace{6cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!45,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[draw,rounded corners,align=center,text width=4.7cm,inner sep=6pt]
 (a) at (0,0) {At most $O(E)$ successful pushes\\in one phase};
\node[draw,rounded corners,align=center,text width=4.7cm,inner sep=6pt]
 (b) at (6.2,0) {At most $O(V)$ path work\\per successful push};
\node[note] at (3.1,0) {times};
\node[draw,rounded corners,align=center,fill=blue!7,text width=5cm,inner sep=6pt]
 (c) at (3.1,-1.8) {$O(VE)$ work per phase};
\draw[ar] (a.south)--(c.north west);
\draw[ar] (b.south)--(c.north east);
\node[note,align=center] at (3.1,-3.2)
 {At most $O(V)$ phases\\[4pt]therefore total time $O(V^2E)$.};

\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Multiplying `O(V)` phases by `O(VE)` work per phase gives Dinic's general
`O(V^2*E)` time bound. BFS and pointer initialization cost `O(V+E)` per phase,
which fit this bound for a nonempty graph. With no edges, one BFS immediately
returns flow zero in `O(V)` time. The graph, levels, pointers, and path stacks
use `O(V+E)` memory.

The bound explains both implementation choices: sending a full bottleneck
avoids one operation per unit of capacity, and retaining current pointers
avoids repeating failed searches within a phase.

# Minimum cut: its capacity equals the maximum flow

A cut partitions vertices into `S` containing `s` and its complement `T`
containing `t`. Its capacity is the sum of **input capacities** of edges
pointing from `S` into `T`. Edges from `T` into `S` are not added.

**Max-flow min-cut theorem.** The largest feasible flow value equals the
smallest cut capacity. We will prove both directions: every cut bounds every
flow from above, and the final residual search finds a cut whose capacity
equals the flow we have already sent.


```{=latex}
% The source side and the minimum cut
\Needspace{7cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!40,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\fill[blue!6,rounded corners] (-.7,-1.7) rectangle (.7,1.7);

\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {1};
\node[nd] (a) at (3,1.2) {2};
\node[nd] (b) at (3,-1.2) {3};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (6,0) {4};
\draw[->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black] (s)--node[lab] {3/3} (a);
\draw[->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black] (s)--node[lab] {2/2} (b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab] {1/1} (b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab] {2/2} (t);
\draw[ar] (b)--node[lab] {3/4} (t);
\draw[orange!75!black,dashed,thick] (1.2,-1.8)--(1.2,1.8);
\node[note] at (0,2.2) {$S=\{1\}$};
\node[note] at (4.5,2.2) {$T=\{2,3,4\}$};
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=4.2cm] at (7.1,0)
 {Crossing input capacities: $3+2=5$.\\[5pt]
  Flow value: 5.\\
  Edge $3\to4$ stays inside $T$ and does not count.};

\node[note,align=center] at (3,-2.5) {Labels are input flow/capacity. The orange input edges leave the source side.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```


Conservation inside `S` cancels all internal flows. Hence the value of any
feasible flow is

```text
flow value = flow from S to T - flow from T to S
           <= capacity from S to T
```

Every cut is therefore an upper bound. After maximum flow, let `S` be all
vertices reachable from `s` using positive residual edges. The sink is outside
`S`, otherwise another augmentation would exist. Two facts now hold:

1. Every input edge from `S` to `T` is saturated. Otherwise its forward
   residual edge would make its destination reachable.
2. Every input edge from `T` to `S` carries zero flow. Otherwise its backward
   residual edge would make its other endpoint reachable.

The next figure uses two distinct input edges, one in each direction.
On the right, both residual arrows point from `S` to `T`, but have different
roles: the solid gray arrow would add flow to the outgoing input edge;
the dashed orange arrow would cancel flow on the incoming input edge.
Their labels show why both have zero capacity here.


```{=latex}
% Why neither kind of residual crossing is available
\Needspace{6cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!40,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[note] at (1.6,1.9) {Input flows across the cut};
\node[note] at (7.4,1.9) {Attempts to leave $S$ in the residual graph};
\node[nd,fill=blue!8] (a) at (0,0) {$u$};
\node[nd] (b) at (3.2,0) {$v$};
\draw[ar] (a) to[bend left=30] node[lab,above] {$f=c$} (b);
\draw[ar] (b) to[bend left=30] node[lab,below] {$f=0$} (a);
\node[note] at (0,-1.4) {$u$ in $S$};
\node[note] at (3.2,-1.4) {$v$ in $T$};
\node[nd,fill=blue!8] (c) at (5.6,0) {$u$};
\node[nd] (d) at (9.2,0) {$v$};
\draw[ar] (c) to[bend left=30] node[lab,above] {$c-f=0$} (d);
\draw[undo] (c) to[bend right=30] node[lab,below] {$f=0$} (d);
\node[note,align=center] at (7.4,-1.6)
 {Solid gray: forward permission, capacity 0.\\
  Dashed orange: cancellation permission, capacity 0.};

\node[note,align=center] at (4.6,-2.8) {Both zero-capacity residual attempts are unusable; neither makes $v$ reachable.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```


Substitute these facts into the displayed equality: the flow value equals
this cut's capacity. This proves the **max-flow min-cut theorem**:

```{=latex}
\Needspace{4cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}
\node[draw=blue!65!black,very thick,rounded corners,fill=blue!6,
      inner sep=12pt,align=center]
 {\textbf{Max-flow min-cut theorem}\\[9pt]
  $\displaystyle
    \text{maximum flow value}=\text{minimum cut capacity}$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

Why are both optimal? No feasible flow can exceed this cut's capacity, so
our flow is maximum. No cut can have capacity below our flow's value, so
this cut is minimum. The absence of incoming flow is needed as well as the
saturation of outgoing edges to obtain the equality.

For the opening example, `S = {1}` and `T = {2,3,4}`. The crossing input
capacities are `3` and `2`, totaling `5`. Edge `3 -> 4` still has unused
capacity, but both its endpoints are in `T`; that does not affect the cut.
Thus **maximum flow value = minimum cut capacity = 5**.

One BFS computes `S` in `O(V+E)` time. For its capacity, sum original capacities
across the partition, rather than summing residual capacities (which are zero
on the forward crossing edges). Minimum cuts need not be unique.


# Dinic: complete reusable implementations

Both versions use 0-based vertices and nonnegative integer capacities.
`add_edge(u, v, c)` returns the forward residual ID. `max_flow(s, t)` mutates
the residual graph and returns the **additional** flow sent by that call;
a second call without graph changes returns `0`. `reachable(s)` returns a
Boolean array for the current residual graph. Call it after maximum flow to
extract a minimum cut.

The C++ version uses `long long` for capacities and totals. Its caller must
keep total capacities and answers within that type. The Python integers do
not have this overflow limit. Neither version uses recursion.

## Small API example

This is a three-vertex network with a bottleneck of `2`. It illustrates the
structure's operations without an exercise input/output wrapper.

```cpp
Dinic network(3);
int edge = network.add_edge(0, 1, 4);
network.add_edge(1, 2, 2);
long long value = network.max_flow(0, 2);  // 2
long long used = network.edges[edge ^ 1].cap;  // 2
std::vector<bool> side = network.reachable(0);  // true, true, false
```

```python
network = Dinic(3)
edge = network.add_edge(0, 1, 4)
network.add_edge(1, 2, 2)
value = network.max_flow(0, 2)         # 2
used = network.cap[edge ^ 1]           # 2
side = network.reachable(0)           # [True, True, False]
```
