# Matching: a concrete reassignment

We now turn from routing amounts through a network to assigning individual
resources. Suppose people request appointment slots. A person may accept
several slots, but can receive at most one; each slot can serve at most one
person. We want to accommodate as many people as possible. A locally valid
assignment may prevent someone else from getting a slot, so we may need to
reassign a person who was already accommodated.

Represent the possibilities by a **bipartite graph**: people are the left
vertices, slots are the right vertices, and an edge means that this person
accepts this slot. Every edge joins the two different sides. The edges here
describe compatibility; their drawing direction has no meaning.

A **matching** is a selection of edges with no shared endpoint: no person
or slot is used twice. Its size is the number of selected pairs. A **maximum
matching** has the largest possible size; it need not match every vertex.
A vertex is **free**, or **unmatched**, if no selected edge touches it.

The connection with flow is the idea of a reversible choice. We can remove
an existing assignment as part of a larger rearrangement that adds one more
pair overall. Let us see exactly how this works before describing the
search algorithm.

Take two people, L1 and L2, and two slots, R1 and R2. L1 accepts either slot;
L2 accepts only R1. Initially, assign R1 to L1:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=10mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={thick},mt/.style={very thick,blue!65!black}]
\node[nd] (a) at (0,1) {L1};
\node[nd] (b) at (0,-1) {L2};
\node[nd] (c) at (4,1) {R1};
\node[nd] (d) at (4,-1) {R2};
\draw[mt] (a)--(c);
\draw[ar] (a)--(d);
\draw[ar] (b)--(c);
\node[align=left,anchor=west] at (5,0)
 {L1 can take R1 or R2.\\L2 can take only R1.\\Blue: first choose L1--R1.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

The initial choice `L1--R1` blocks L2 if we refuse to change it. R2 is still
free, but L2 cannot take it directly. We can nevertheless accommodate L2 by
moving L1 to R2. To find that rearrangement, search this route:

```text
L2 -> R1 -> L1 -> R2
```


```{=latex}
% An alternating path to a free right vertex
\Needspace{4cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!40,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[nd,fill=blue!8] (a) at (0,0) {L2};
\node[nd] (b) at (3,0) {R1};
\node[nd] (c) at (6,0) {L1};
\node[nd,fill=green!15] (d) at (9,0) {R2};
\draw[blue] (a)--node[lab,above=4mm]{unused}(b);
\draw[undo] (b)--node[lab,above=4mm]{matched: undo}(c);
\draw[blue] (c)--node[lab,above=4mm]{unused}(d);
\node[note] at (0,-.9) {free left};
\node[note] at (9,-.9) {free right};

\node[note,align=center] at (4.5,-1.8) {Follow unused edges left to right, and the occupied edge back to its owner.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```


Start at unmatched L2. Traverse an unused edge to R1, then its currently
matched edge backward to L1, then an unused edge to unmatched R2. Flip the
three edges: remove `L1--R1`, add `L2--R1` and `L1--R2`. The size rises from
`1` to `2` and no vertex is used twice.


```{=latex}
% The two pairs after flipping the alternating path
\Needspace{5cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!40,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[nd] (a) at (0,1) {L1};
\node[nd] (b) at (0,-1) {L2};
\node[nd] (c) at (4,1) {R1};
\node[nd] (d) at (4,-1) {R2};
\draw[thick,draw=black!40] (a)--(c);
\draw[very thick,draw=green!40!black] (a)--(d);
\draw[very thick,draw=green!40!black] (b)--(c);
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=5cm] at (5.1,0)
 {Remove L1--R1.\\[4pt]
  Add L1--R2 and L2--R1.\\[4pt]
  Both sides now use every vertex once.};

\node[note,align=center] at (2,-2) {Green edges form the new matching of size 2.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```


This is an **augmenting alternating path**. Its edges alternate between
unused and matched, starting and ending with unused edges. It connects a free
left vertex to a free right vertex and increases the matching size by one.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{8cm}
```

## Search with owners and predecessors

The search answers a concrete question: **can we accommodate one more person
by moving some current assignments?** It has two separate stages. First find
a possible rearrangement without changing any assignment. If it reaches a
free slot, apply the complete rearrangement.

### What the arrays and queue remember

Continue with L1 assigned to R1 and L2 still free. Here is the complete
starting state again:

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=9mm,fill=white},
 note/.style={font=\small,align=left}]
\node[nd] (l1) at (0,1) {L1};
\node[nd,fill=blue!8] (l2) at (0,-1) {L2};
\node[nd] (r1) at (3.5,1) {R1};
\node[nd,fill=green!15] (r2) at (3.5,-1) {R2};
\draw[very thick,blue!65!black] (l1)--(r1);
\draw[thick,black!60] (l1)--(r2);
\draw[thick,black!60] (l2)--(r1);
\node[note,anchor=west] at (5,0)
 {Current partners:\\[4pt]
  left[L1] = R1; left[L2] = -1.\\
  right[R1] = L1; right[R2] = -1.\\[4pt]
  Blue edge: assigned. Other edges: compatible.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

`left[u]` is person `u`'s current slot. `right[v]` is slot `v`'s current
owner. The value `-1` means no partner. The labels L1 and R1 name different
vertices; in the implementation each side has its own 0-based IDs.

For one search, we also need:

- **`queue`: people whose possible slots still need inspection.** Initially
  it contains only the free person L2. We may later add an occupied slot's
  owner, to find out whether that person can move elsewhere.
- **`previous[v]`: the person from whom we first reached slot `v`.** It
  records a possible new owner, without assigning the slot yet. Initially
  every entry is `-1`, meaning the slot has not been visited by this search.
- **`seen[u]`: whether person `u` has already been enqueued.** This prevents
  repeated exploration of the same person's options.

In particular, `right[R1]` and `previous[R1]` answer different questions:
**who owns R1 now**, and **who might take R1 in this rearrangement**.

### Follow the example without changing the matching

**Start:** `queue = [L2]`. All `previous` entries are `-1`.

**Inspect L2:** remove L2 from the queue. Its only possible slot is R1.
Record `previous[R1] = L2`. But `right[R1] = L1`: R1 is occupied. We cannot
finish yet, so enqueue L1 to look for somewhere its current owner could move.
Now `queue = [L1]`. The assignment L1--R1 is still unchanged.

**Inspect L1:** remove L1 from the queue. R1 was already visited, so skip it.
Its other possible slot is R2. Record `previous[R2] = L1`. Since
`right[R2] = -1`, R2 is free: we have found an endpoint for the rearrangement.

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 lab/.style={font=\small,fill=white,inner sep=2pt}]
\node[nd,fill=blue!8] (a) at (0,0) {L2};
\node[nd] (b) at (3,0) {R1};
\node[nd] (c) at (6,0) {L1};
\node[nd,fill=green!15] (d) at (9,0) {R2};
\draw[->,very thick,blue!65!black] (a)--node[lab,above=4mm]{possible new pair}(b);
\draw[->,thick,dashed,orange!75!black] (b)--node[lab,above=4mm]{current owner}(c);
\draw[->,very thick,blue!65!black] (c)--node[lab,above=4mm]{possible new pair}(d);
\node[font=\small,align=center] at (4.5,-1)
 {L2 could take R1 if L1 moves. L1 can move to free R2.\\
  Discovery is complete; no assignment has changed yet.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

### Apply the rearrangement from the free slot backward

Start with the free slot R2. `previous[R2] = L1` tells us to give it to L1.
Before doing that, remember L1's old slot, R1: that is the next slot whose
new owner we must set. Then `previous[R1] = L2` tells us to give R1 to L2.
L2 had no old slot, so we are finished.

```{=latex}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 lab/.style={font=\small,fill=white,inner sep=2pt}]
\node[nd,fill=green!15] (a) at (0,0) {R2};
\node[nd] (b) at (2.7,0) {L1};
\node[nd] (c) at (5.4,0) {R1};
\node[nd] (d) at (8.1,0) {L2};
\node[draw,minimum width=10mm,minimum height=8mm] (e) at (10.8,0) {$-1$};
\draw[->,thick,blue!65!black] (a)--node[lab,above=4mm]{previous}(b);
\draw[->,thick] (b)--node[lab,above=4mm]{old slot}(c);
\draw[->,thick,blue!65!black] (c)--node[lab,above=4mm]{previous}(d);
\draw[->,thick] (d)--node[lab,above=4mm]{old slot}(e);
\node[font=\small,align=center] at (5.4,-1)
 {Give R2 to L1, then R1 to L2. Stop at the person who had no old slot.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

These are exactly the reconstruction steps in the implementation:

```text
v = the free slot found by the search
while v != -1:
    u = previous[v]       # person who will take this slot
    old = left[u]         # save that person's old slot first
    left[u] = v
    right[v] = u
    v = old               # continue with the slot just released
```

After the whole flip:

```text
left[L1] = R2     right[R2] = L1
left[L2] = R1     right[R1] = L2
```

Treat the complete flip as one operation. Between its individual assignments,
partner arrays may temporarily disagree; after it finishes they agree again.
The matching has gained one pair while keeping every previous person matched.

### Two more pairs, found in two visual passes

We will keep **the complete graph and the same vertex positions in every
picture**. There are four people, A, B, C, D, and four slots. A can take
R1, R3, or R4; B can take R2 or R3; C accepts only R1; D accepts only R2.

Process A, B, C, D in that order. First assign A to R1 and B to R2. We now
have two pairs. The next two searches, from C and then D, will find the two
missing pairs. Here a **pass** means one search and its resulting
rearrangement; it is not a Dinic phase.

In each picture, gray edges show compatibility and **thick black edges
show the current matching**. During a search, a **solid blue arrow proposes
a new pair**; a **dashed orange arrow returns from an occupied slot to its
current owner**. The orange vertex is the current search position. The
matching changes only after reaching a free slot; the resulting pairs are
then drawn in green.

**Pass 1: start from C, keeping A--R1 and B--R2.**

**Why does one turn per starting person suffice?**
The searches may revisit earlier people to move their assignments, as we
just saw with B and A. The real question is: **if someone's search fails,
can a later rearrangement make it worth trying again?**

Consider this different graph, processed in the order A, D, B, C.
A, D, and B each accept only R1 or R2. C accepts R2 or R3. First assign
A--R1 and D--R2.

**1. B fails after exploring a closed region.** B tries both occupied
slots, then all alternatives of their owners A and D:

The failure establishes two facts about the shaded region: **every slot
inside is occupied**, and **none of its people accepts a slot outside**.
Changing the assignments elsewhere cannot create a missing compatibility

A keeps R1.\\
D keeps R2.\\

\node[font=\small,align=center] at (2,-5.1) {Shaded region: the vertices reached by B\textquotesingle s failed search.\\Black lines: assigned pairs; orange arrows follow assignments backward.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

This is the general reason we do not retry failed roots. After an exhaustive
failure, the reached region has no free slot and no alternating exit. Any
later successful augmenting path must avoid it, so its assignments stay
unchanged. Repeating the failed search would meet the same obstruction.

For a successful root, no retry is needed either: future augmentations may
move that person to another slot, but never leave them unmatched. Thus we
can start once from each person while still revisiting earlier matched
people inside the searches.

\newpage
```

## Why matching is a flow problem too

Create a source, a sink, and distinct vertices for both sides. Add:

| Edge family | Capacity |
| --- | --- |
| Source to every left vertex | 1 |
| Each allowed left-right pair | 1 |
| Every right vertex to sink | 1 |


```{=latex}
% The matching as a unit-capacity flow network
\Needspace{6cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,draw=black!65},
 blue/.style={->,very thick,draw=blue!65!black},
 undo/.style={->,very thick,draw=orange!75!black,dashed},
 muted/.style={->,thick,draw=black!40,dashed},
 lab/.style={fill=white,inner sep=2pt,font=\small},
 note/.style={align=left,font=\small},
 cell/.style={draw,minimum width=14mm,minimum height=8mm,fill=white}]

\node[nd,fill=orange!20] (s) at (0,0) {$s$};
\node[nd] (a) at (2.3,1.2) {L1};
\node[nd] (b) at (2.3,-1.2) {L2};
\node[nd] (c) at (5,1.2) {R1};
\node[nd] (d) at (5,-1.2) {R2};
\node[nd,fill=green!20] (t) at (7.3,0) {$t$};
\draw[blue] (s)--node[lab]{1}(a);
\draw[blue] (s)--node[lab]{1}(b);
\draw[ar] (a)--node[lab]{1}(c);
\draw[blue] (a)--node[lab,pos=.65]{1}(d);
\draw[blue] (b)--node[lab,pos=.65]{1}(c);
\draw[blue] (c)--node[lab]{1}(t);
\draw[blue] (d)--node[lab]{1}(t);
\node[note,anchor=west,text width=3.7cm] at (8.4,0)
 {Every capacity is 1.\\[5pt]
  Blue routes send 2 units and select 2 pairs.};

\node[note,align=center] at (3.65,-2.4) {Source and sink edges prevent either side from using one vertex twice.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```


**Why can a person receive at most one slot?** Take L1. Its only incoming
input edge is `s -> L1`, of capacity 1. Conservation at L1 says that the
sum sent to all its possible slots equals the amount received from `s`.
So L1 can send at most 1 in total. It cannot send 1 to R1 and another 1 to
R2: that would require receiving 2 through an edge of capacity 1.

**Why can a slot serve at most one person?** Take R1. Its only outgoing
input edge is `R1 -> t`, of capacity 1. Conservation at R1 says that the
sum received from all people equals the amount sent to `t`. So R1 can
receive at most 1 in total, even if several people accept it.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{5cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[>=Latex,
 nd/.style={circle,draw,minimum size=8mm,fill=white},
 ar/.style={->,thick,black!65},
 boundedge/.style={->,very thick,blue!65!black},
 lab/.style={font=\small,fill=white,inner sep=2pt}]
\node[nd] (s) at (0,0) {$s$};
\node[nd] (l) at (2,0) {L1};
\node[nd] (r1) at (4,1) {R1};
\node[nd] (r2) at (4,-1) {R2};
\draw[boundedge] (s)--node[lab,above=4mm]{capacity 1}(l);
\draw[ar] (l)--node[lab,above]{$x$}(r1);
\draw[ar] (l)--node[lab,below]{$y$}(r2);
\node[font=\small] at (2,-1.8) {L1: $x+y\leq 1$.};
\node[nd] (l1) at (7,1) {L1};
\node[nd] (l2) at (7,-1) {L2};
\node[nd] (r) at (9,0) {R1};
\node[nd] (t) at (11,0) {$t$};
\draw[ar] (l1)--node[lab,above]{$x$}(r);
\draw[ar] (l2)--node[lab,below]{$y$}(r);
\draw[boundedge] (r)--node[lab,above=4mm]{capacity 1}(t);
\node[font=\small] at (9,-1.8) {R1: $x+y\leq 1$.};
\node[font=\small] at (5.5,-2.6)
 {Two local views. Labels $x,y$ are flows; blue labels are capacities.};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}
```

**Why do we get whole pairs rather than fractions?** Dinic starts with
zero flow. All capacities here are integers, so every residual capacity and
every path bottleneck is an integer. Adding or cancelling that amount keeps
all input flows integral. Since every middle edge has capacity 1, its flow
is therefore either 0 or 1. We select exactly the pairs whose middle edge
carries 1. The two constraints above ensure that no person or slot belongs
to two selected pairs. These pairs form a matching, and their count equals
the flow value.

**How does a matching give a flow in the other direction?** For each pair
`L--R` in a matching, send one unit along `s -> L -> R -> t`. Because no
person or slot is repeated, these routes never exceed any capacity.
Conservation holds, and a matching of `k` pairs gives a feasible flow of
value `k`. In the complete network at the start of this subsection, the
two selected pairs give the routes
`s -> L1 -> R2 -> t` and `s -> L2 -> R1 -> t`.

Thus any matching can be turned into a flow of the same value, and the
maximum integral flow returned by Dinic can be turned into a matching of
the same size. Neither optimum can exceed the other:
**maximum matching size = maximum flow value in this constructed network**.

The matched step from R1 to L1 is exactly a reverse residual step. Our direct
matching search leaves the source and sink implicit. It uses BFS augmenting
paths without Dinic's blocking-flow phases; the two algorithms share the
residual principle but organize their searches differently.

# Matching: complete reusable implementations

`add_edge(u, v)` adds a permitted pair, with 0-based IDs on each side.
`maximum_matching()` returns `(left, right)` pairs and leaves both partner
arrays available. The implementation uses an explicit queue and path flip,
so Python does not need recursive calls. Calling the method again without
adding edges preserves the matching.

For `L` left vertices, `R` right vertices, and `E` allowed pairs, each search
costs `O(E+L+R)`, including clearing its arrays. There are at most `L` searches,
so total time is `O(L*(E+L+R))` and storage is `O(E+L+R)`. At the exercise's
`L,R <= 500`, this direct approach is appropriate. For much larger bipartite
graphs, Hopcroft-Karp batches shortest augmenting paths; it is a later tool.

```cpp
BipartiteMatching matching(2, 2);
matching.add_edge(0, 0);
matching.add_edge(0, 1);
matching.add_edge(1, 0);
auto pairs = matching.maximum_matching();  // {(0, 1), (1, 0)}
```

```python
matching = BipartiteMatching(2, 2)
matching.add_edge(0, 0)
matching.add_edge(0, 1)
matching.add_edge(1, 0)
pairs = matching.maximum_matching()       # [(0, 1), (1, 0)]
```

## Recognize a suitable model

Capacity restrictions, conserved quantities passing through junctions, and
maximizing total delivery suggest flow. Choosing distinct pairs across two
sides suggests matching. In both settings, a locally convenient choice can
block later choices, and residual searches allow reassignment.

A capacity limits an amount; it is not a cost or a distance. Ordinary maximum
flow does not minimize travel cost. Before implementing, identify the source,
the sink, the capacity of each edge, and the quantity one unit represents.
For matching, identify both sides and which pairs are legal.

## Useful checks and failure cases

| Case | Property to check |
| --- | --- |
| Single edge of capacity 7 | Value is 7, not 1 |
| Unreachable sink, or zero-capacity edges | Value is 0 |
| Four-vertex opening network | Rebuild BFS; total is 5 |
| Six-vertex cancellation network | Reverse residuals allow total 2 |
| Parallel and opposite input edges | Every input edge keeps its own pair |
| Many capacities of a billion | C++ totals use 64-bit integers |
| A long directed chain | Explicit stack works without recursion |
| Two left vertices competing for one right | Matching size is 1 |
| L1 connects to R1/R2, L2 only to R1 | Reassignment finds size 2 |
| No matching edges | Empty pair list |

For small flow graphs, enumerate every source-side subset containing `s` but
not `t`, compute its input cut capacity, and compare the minimum with Dinic.
Also verify capacities, junction conservation, and the returned cut. For
matching, use an exhaustive small search and validate every returned pair,
its membership in the input, and endpoint uniqueness.

Before submitting, check both residual updates, pointer resets per phase,
positive-residual BFS, independent matching IDs, and output ordering required
by the statement. Public `solve.*` files are stubs; keep personal attempts
in the private submissions overlay.
